messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Factory Worker
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Proximity: Physical proximity, Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Heavy Makeup: heavy make-up, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amina is a 42-year-old divorced African American woman who works long shifts on a factory floor, and she came to treatment after months of feeling as though her life had narrowed to getting through work, getting home, and staying on guard. Years earlier, she was detained and tortured. She describes being held in a small room where other bodies were forced close to hers, where names were shouted back and forth by the men who controlled the space, and where the air carried a distinct odor she can still summon against her will. The weather that day had been heavy and close, the kind of humid pressure before a storm that now turns her stomach. What stays with her is not a coherent story but fragments: the smell, the sense of bodies pressing near, the sound of names, and the certainty that she had no control over what happened to her own body.

In the aftermath, Amina began to notice that certain moments in ordinary life were not ordinary to her. On crowded bus rides or when a coworker at the factory leaned too near to speak over the machinery, her whole body stiffened before she had time to think. If she heard a name that resembled one she associates with the men who hurt her, or if the day turned hot and storm-heavy, she would feel pulled sharply backward into the event. She says that when those things happen, she can sometimes smell again what she smelled then, and the memory arrives with such force and strangeness that it feels unreal, almost as if it happened to somebody else. Because those cues seem to appear anywhere, she has come to see the world as dangerous in a constant, ambient way, not just in obviously unsafe places.

That sense of danger has spread into her view of herself. Amina had once thought of herself as strong, capable, and able to endure hard work without losing her footing. Now she is shaken by how little warning she seems to have before her body reacts. She has come to believe she can no longer trust her own body, and that she is no longer capable in the way she once was. When she startles violently at ordinary noises in the plant or finds herself listening at night for any sound that might mean someone is entering her apartment, it confirms for her that the danger is real and that she has been permanently changed by it. The more she scans, the more she notices sounds, footsteps, weather shifts, and people standing too close; those same things now register immediately as signs of threat.

Over time she has built her days around trying not to be overtaken. She wears heavy makeup every day, describing it less as vanity than as a way to feel hidden and armoured. She avoids clothes that resemble what she wore during the torture, even when that makes getting dressed for work more difficult. She keeps her mind occupied constantly—television on in the background, music in her headphones after work, repetitive mental lists on the assembly line—because any quiet moment risks bringing back the smell, the unreal quality of the memory, and the sickening sense that the past is not fully past. These habits make sense to her because she is convinced that if she lets down her guard or allows herself to think directly about what happened, she will lose control altogether.

At the factory, the cycle is especially tight. The closeness of other workers, shouted names over machinery, and the metallic smells in the heat of the building can all act as triggers. She becomes intensely alert, jumping at routine noises and monitoring every movement around her. In that state, the memory intrudes in sensory flashes rather than narrative form, and because it feels alien and unbelievable even while it is vividly present, she tries harder to push it away by overfocusing on tasks, avoiding certain uniforms and fabrics, and checking how she looks behind a mask of makeup before her shift. Yet the effort to keep the memory at bay seems only to leave it more fragmented and more startling when it returns.

At home, nights are the worst. Amina listens for entry sounds with an intensity that leaves her exhausted. A settling radiator, footsteps in the hallway, rain building in humid weather—each can make her body jerk before she has formed a thought. The startle itself frightens her; it seems proof that her body is unreliable and that she is living in a world where danger can come through any door. That fear makes the triggers feel even more potent and broadens the range of what she avoids. By the time she sought help, she was missing social invitations, feeling increasingly cut off, and struggling to keep steady at work because so much energy went into staying occupied and braced.

She came in after realizing that she was no longer simply remembering what had been done to her; she was organizing her whole life around not feeling it and still being ambushed by it. What frightens her most is the belief that the torture has broken something permanent in her—that her body will always react first, that ordinary closeness and ordinary weather will always carry the past inside them. What she hopes, cautiously, is that she might find a way to live without having to hide from names, from crowds, from heat in the air, and from her own memory.
